summary: Describes the correct procedure for incrementally updating the Internet checksum when only part of a packet changes, so it need not be recomputed from scratch. It replaces the description in RFC 1071. It is an implementation technique, not a standard.

eli5.summary: If you change one number in a long sum, you do not redo everything. You just fix the total by the difference.

questions: how to update ip checksum after changing a field
how to update ip checksum after changing ttl
what is wrong with the rfc 1071 checksum update
subtitle: A corrected recipe for patching the Internet checksum when only one field of a packet changes.

tldr.problem: When a router changes one field of an IP header, such as the TTL, recomputing the whole checksum is wasteful, and the update equation in RFC 1071 is hard to turn into working code.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the update on the stored value, the complement of the checksum, using one's complement arithmetic, and gives C code that adds 1 or 256 to the checksum field when the TTL drops by one.
tldr.outcome: It is an implementation technique, not a standard. It is meant to replace the description in RFC 1071 and is itself updated by RFC 1624.

facts.label: TTL decrement of one
facts.value: Add 1 or 256 to the checksum field

today: RFC 1141 is Informational and is updated by RFC 1624. It is intended to replace the incremental update description in RFC 1071, and the unit metadata lists it as updating that RFC.

sections.title: Why an Update Was Needed
sections.content:
RFC 1071 describes a way to update the checksum in an IP header without recomputing it completely. It recommends the equation C' = C + (-m) + m' = C + (m' - m), where C is the original checksum and m and m' are the old and new values of the changed byte.

This memo says the equation is correct but not very useful. It updates C, while the value stored in the checksum field is ~C, the complement. It also does not make clear that all arithmetic, including the unary negation, must be done in one's complement, so it is hard to build working code from it.
sections.eli5: The old recipe was right, but it told you how to fix a number that nobody writes down, and it did not say which kind of adding to use. This note fixes both problems.

sections.title: The Corrected Update Rule
sections.content:
For 2's complement machines, the memo gives the useful calculation as ~C' = ~(C + (-m) + m') = ~C + (m - m') = ~C + m + ~m'. This works directly on the value stored in the packet and uses one's complement addition.

The memo points to the common case of updating the IP TTL field. Subtracting one from the TTL means adding 1 or 256 to the checksum field, as appropriate, using one's complement addition.
sections.eli5: Take the number on the label, add the small difference, and carry any overflow back around. That gives the new label without redoing all the work.

sections.title: C Examples for the TTL
sections.content:
The first example is a big-endian, non-portable C snippet. It decrements the TTL, adds 0x100 to the checksum, and folds the carry back in. The memo notes that this special case can be optimized in many ways, for instance by bundling the TTL update with the TTL check, and that compiler mileage may vary.

The second example, UpdateTTL, is more general. It lowers the TTL by n seconds, adds the old 16-bit word to the complement of the new one and to the stored checksum, then folds the carries twice before storing the result.
sections.eli5: There are two little programs. One handles taking exactly one off the counter, and the other handles taking off any amount.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that security issues are not addressed. It describes only a faster way to keep an existing checksum correct after a field changes.
sections.eli5: This note is only about doing the arithmetic right. It does not say anything about keeping secrets or stopping bad guys.

references.text: RFC 1071, the Internet checksum document whose incremental update description this memo is intended to replace.
